title: Energy in Living Things
seo_title: Life Sciences 11: Energy in Living Things Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Organisms transform energy: enzymes, photosynthesis and cellular respiration, ATP, and the relationship between the two processes. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Life Sciences 11)
meta_desc: Free Life Sciences 11 worksheets (BC Curriculum): enzymes, photosynthesis, respiration and ATP. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it.
key_sub: ATP carries energy in the cell.
body_html:
How to think about it

Photosynthesis in chloroplasts: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Cellular respiration in mitochondria: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP). Without oxygen, cells use fermentation, which makes much less ATP.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. Each enzyme fits its substrate at the active site; high temperature or the wrong pH can denature it.

Example

Which gas is released by photosynthesis?

Plants give it off in light.

Answer: oxygen

Example

What happens to an enzyme at 70 °C?

Its shape changes.

Answer: it is denatured and stops working

Common mistakes

  • Thinking plants do not respire.
  • Thinking enzymes are used up.
  • Mixing up the reactants and products of the two processes.

faq.q: Where does the energy in ATP come from?
faq.a: From breaking down glucose in cellular respiration.

faq.q: Why do muscles make lactic acid?
faq.a: When oxygen is short, they use fermentation.

items.q: What is made in anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
items.e: Yeast makes ethanol and CO₂ instead.

items.q: How does a competitive inhibitor work?
c: it binds to the active site, so substrate cannot bind
it binds elsewhere and changes the active site shape
items.e: Adding more substrate reduces its effect.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) take place?
c: in the stroma of the chloroplast
items.e: CO₂ is fixed by the enzyme RuBisCO.

items.q: What do ligases do?
c: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds
transferring a group from one substrate to another
catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates
items.e: Ligases: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds.

items.q: Why does increasing temperature (below the optimum) speed up an enzyme reaction?
c: molecules have more kinetic energy, so there are more successful collisions
items.e: More enzyme–substrate complexes form.

items.q: Which class of enzymes is responsible for joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds?
items.e: Ligases: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds.

items.q: Catalase releases 18 mL of oxygen in the first 30 s. Calculate the mean rate in mL per minute.
What is the substrate of amylase?
items.e: Amylase gives maltose.

items.q: A starch solution takes 64 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
Why does each enzyme work on only one substrate?
c: enzymes are used up after one reaction
enzymes are too large for other substrates
the active site has a shape that fits only that substrate
all substrates have the same shape
items.e: Lock-and-key and induced-fit models.

items.q: What happens to an enzyme at a very high temperature?
c: it is denatured: the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits
items.e: Bonds holding the shape break.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 25 units and at 35 °C it is 50 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 36 units and at 35 °C it is 48 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
Which factor would NOT increase the rate of photosynthesis in a plant already in bright light at 25 °C with low CO₂?
c: a slightly warmer temperature up to the optimum
items.e: When CO₂ is limiting, extra light makes no difference.

items.q: Which class of enzymes is responsible for catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates?
items.e: Oxidoreductases: catalyzing oxidation and reduction between two substrates.

items.q: Which class of enzymes is responsible for transferring a group from one substrate to another?
items.e: Transferases: transferring a group from one substrate to another.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 18 units and at 35 °C it is 45 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
What is the induced-fit model?
c: the substrate changes into the enzyme
the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds
items.e: This puts strain on the substrate's bonds.

items.q: A starch solution takes 50 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
A starch solution takes 40 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
How many ATP and NADPH are needed to fix one molecule of CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
items.e: Six turns make one glucose: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

items.q: What is the name for the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP?
items.e: RuBisCO: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP.

items.q: What is an enzyme?
c: a lipid in the cell membrane
a protein that is a biological catalyst
items.e: Enzymes speed up reactions and are not used up.

items.q: What is PS I?
c: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP
the splitting of water that releases oxygen
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700)
large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves
items.e: PS I: a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700).

items.q: What is the law of limiting factors?
c: the largest factor controls the rate
the rate is limited by the factor that is nearest its minimum value
items.e: Proposed by Blackman.

items.q: Where does the oxygen given out in photosynthesis come from?
items.e: Shown with heavy-oxygen isotopes.

items.q: What is photolysis?
c: light splitting water into protons, electrons and oxygen
items.e: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂.

items.q: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
c: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ ATP)
items.e: It releases energy as ATP.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 2.0 cm and the solvent moves 12 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
About how many ATP are made from one glucose in aerobic respiration?
items.e: Anaerobic respiration gives only 2.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle take place?
c: in the stroma of the chloroplast
items.e: It uses ATP and NADPH.

items.q: What is photolysis?
c: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP
the splitting of water that releases oxygen
the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700)
items.e: Photolysis: the splitting of water that releases oxygen.

items.q: Who showed that sunlight is needed for plants to purify air?
items.e: He used an aquatic plant in light and dark.

items.q: Which photosystem is used in cyclic photophosphorylation?
c: both PS I and PS II
items.e: It makes ATP but no NADPH or O₂.

items.q: What is the name for the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar?
items.e: Calvin cycle: the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar.

items.q: What is RuBisCO?
c: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP
RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 680 nm (P680)
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700)
items.e: RuBisCO: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 3.6 cm and the solvent moves 9.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
What is the Z scheme?
c: the zig-zag path of electrons from PS II to PS I in non-cyclic photophosphorylation
items.e: Electrons go up in energy twice.

items.q: What is the name for the splitting of water that releases oxygen?
items.e: Photolysis: the splitting of water that releases oxygen.

items.q: What is the primary CO₂ acceptor in C₄ plants?
items.e: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells.

items.q: Why is potassium hydroxide used in a respirometer?
c: it absorbs the carbon dioxide produced
items.e: So the change in volume is oxygen taken in.

items.q: What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?
items.e: Oxygen combines with electrons and protons to form water.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 8 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 16 ATP.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 2 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 4 ATP.

items.q: Which enzyme makes ATP in the inner mitochondrial membrane?
items.e: Protons flow through it.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 3 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 3 = 6.

items.q: Why is anaerobic respiration much less efficient than aerobic respiration?
c: glucose is only partly broken down, so much less ATP is made
it makes no ATP at all
items.e: Energy is left in lactate or ethanol.

items.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in mammals?
items.e: Pyruvate is reduced, regenerating NAD.

items.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in yeast?
items.e: This is alcoholic fermentation.

items.q: An organism takes in 36 mL of oxygen and gives out 29 mL of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
items.e: RQ = CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in = 0.806 (1.0 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for lipid, about 0.9 for protein).

items.q: An organism takes in 60 mL of oxygen and gives out 43 mL of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
items.e: RQ = CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in = 0.717 (1.0 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for lipid, about 0.9 for protein).

items.q: Where does glycolysis take place?
items.e: Glucose is split into two pyruvate.

items.q: What happens in the link reaction?
c: pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl CoA, releasing CO₂ and reducing NAD
items.e: It takes place in the matrix.

items.q: What is formed when pyruvate enters the mitochondrion?
c: acetyl CoA, with release of CO₂ and NADH
items.e: This is oxidative decarboxylation.

items.q: A competitive inhibitor slows an enzyme. How does it work?
c: it has a similar shape to the substrate and blocks the active site
items.e: Adding more substrate reduces its effect.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 5 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 10 ATP.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 4 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 4 = 8.

items.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) of carbohydrates?
items.e: CO₂ given out = O₂ taken in.

items.q: Where does glycolysis take place?
items.e: Glucose is split into two pyruvate.

items.q: An organism takes in 20 mL of oxygen and gives out 14 mL of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
items.e: RQ = CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in = 0.700 (1.0 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for lipid, about 0.9 for protein).

items.q: What is a limiting factor?
c: the factor that is in shortest supply and so controls the rate
a factor that stops a reaction for ever
the temperature at which an enzyme denatures
the factor that is present in excess
items.e: Light, CO₂ and temperature limit photosynthesis.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 9 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 9 = 18.

items.q: Where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
c: on the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast
items.e: Chlorophyll is in the thylakoids.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 9 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 18 ATP.

items.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
items.e: Glycolysis: the cytoplasm.

items.q: What is photorespiration?
c: a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 680 nm (P680)
RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy
large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves
the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar
items.e: Photorespiration: RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy.

items.q: Where in the cell does the electron transport chain take place?
items.e: The electron transport chain: the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.q: What is PS II?
c: a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 680 nm (P680)
the enzyme that fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells of C₄ plants
RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy
the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar
items.e: PS II: a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 680 nm (P680).

items.q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
c: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in light, with chlorophyll)
items.e: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

items.q: What is the first product of the Krebs cycle?
items.e: Acetyl CoA + oxaloacetic acid → citric acid.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 1 molecule of glucose is broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 2 ATP.

items.q: Where in the cell does fermentation take place?
items.e: Fermentation: the cytoplasm, without oxygen.

items.q: Where do the light reactions of photosynthesis take place?
items.e: The dark reactions are in the stroma.

items.q: Where does the electron transport chain of aerobic respiration take place?
c: on the inner membrane (cristae) of the mitochondrion
items.e: Most ATP is made here.

items.q: Where in the cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
items.e: The Krebs cycle: the mitochondrial matrix.

items.q: What is the end product of glycolysis?
items.e: Glucose → 2 pyruvic acid.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 5 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 5 = 10.

items.q: What is the role of ATP in cells?
c: it carries energy from respiration to reactions that need it
it is the main component of membranes
items.e: ATP → ADP + Pi releases energy.

items.q: What is the name for large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves?
items.e: Kranz anatomy: large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 10 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 20 ATP.

items.q: A water plant gives off 48 bubbles of oxygen in 3 minutes. What is the rate of photosynthesis in bubbles per minute?
items.e: Rate = 48 ÷ 3. Counting bubbles measures the oxygen released.

items.q: At dawn, the rate of photosynthesis is low but rising. What is the limiting factor?
items.e: The limiting factor is the one that, when increased, increases the rate.

items.q: A greenhouse plant has lots of light and water, but the air has little CO<sub>2</sub>. What limits photosynthesis?
items.e: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate.

items.q: Plants in a drought close their stomata. What drops first?
c: the carbon dioxide entering the leaf
items.e: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate.
